WASDI application
Rainfall Anomaly (IMERG)
Wetter or drier than normal, everywhere, every day

A rainfall map shows how much rain fell. This page explains how the WASDI apps turn NASA's satellite rainfall into maps of how unusual that rain is over the last 3, 7 and 30 days. It covers the data, the method, the processing chain, real results, and how to run the apps yourself.

Overview

The same rain means different things in different places

Fifty millimetres of rain in a week is an ordinary week in a rainforest and an exceptional one in a desert. To know whether rain is unusual, you must compare it with what normally falls in that place at that time of year. These apps make that comparison for the whole world, every day, from NASA satellite data.

In this section

0.1Normal rain and the anomaly

The normal is the rain a place usually gets on given calendar days, averaged over many years. It is also called the climatology. The anomaly is the difference between the rain that actually fell and that normal.

Place A · rainy season

50 mm in 7 days

Normal for those 7 days: 60 mm. Anomaly −10 mm, 83% of normal. A slightly dry week.

Place B · dry season

50 mm in 7 days

Normal for those 7 days: 4 mm. Anomaly +46 mm, 1250% of normal. An extraordinary week.

A rain-total map shows both places in the same colour. An anomaly map shows Place A as near normal and Place B as strongly wetter than normal. That is the information you need for flood watch, drought monitoring and agriculture.

0.2What the apps deliver

1Daily rolling mapsThe app imerg_rolling_anomaly runs on a schedule. Every day it makes maps for the last 3, 7 and 30 days, ending on the most recent day NASA has published.
2Two measuresThe anomaly in mm (how much extra or missing water) and the percent of normal (how unusual the period is for that place and season).
3Ready to viewEvery map carries a colour style, so it displays the same way in WASDI and in RISE, the WASDI risk platform, without any setting.

A second app, spatial_anomaly_analyzer, compares any single map with any baseline on demand, and can summarise the result per region. Tab 4 explains how the two apps fit together.

0.3Key terms

TermMeaning on this page
IMERGNASA's Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM: a global rainfall estimate built from many satellites, on a 0.1° grid (about 11 km).
WindowThe run of consecutive days a map covers, for example the last 7 days.
Reference dayThe last day of every window. By default, the most recent day NASA has published.
ObservedRain measured by IMERG over the window, summed day by day.
NormalThe average rain of the same calendar days over 2001–2022, summed over the window.
AnomalyObserved minus normal, in mm. Positive is wetter than normal, negative is drier.
Percent of normalObserved divided by normal, times 100. 100% is exactly normal.
RollingEach day the window moves forward by one day: the newest day enters, the oldest leaves.

The data

Two ingredients from the same satellite record

Observed rain and normal rain both come from NASA's IMERG. Using the same source for both keeps the comparison fair: the observation and its normal are measured the same way.

In this section

1.1IMERG: rain from a constellation of satellites

No single satellite sees the whole Earth all the time. IMERG combines many.

  • Microwave radiometers on low-orbit satellites sense rain fairly directly: raindrops and ice emit and scatter microwaves. They pass over a given place only a few times a day.
  • Infrared imagers on geostationary satellites watch continuously, but only see cloud-top temperature, a weaker clue to rain.
  • The GPM Core Observatory, with a precipitation radar and a microwave radiometer, is the reference that calibrates the other sensors.

IMERG moves the microwave estimates along with cloud motion seen in the infrared, and merges everything into a rain rate every 30 minutes on a 0.1° grid between 60°S and 60°N. Coverage is partial up to the poles. Daily totals add up the 48 half-hours of a UTC day.

1.2Early, Late and Final: speed against accuracy

NASA runs IMERG three times on the same data, each time with more information.

RunAvailable afterCan useUsed here for
Earlyabout 4 hoursonly data before each half-hournot used
Lateabout 14 hoursdata before and after each half-hourobserved rain
Finalabout 3.5 monthsall of the above plus monthly rain-gauge analysesnormal rain

Final is the most accurate but far too slow for monitoring. Late is the best estimate available within a day, so the apps use it for the observations. The normal is built from Final, the best long record.

1.3Observed rain: the daily Late files

NASA publishes one daily Late file per UTC day as a GeoTIFF, available in the WASDI catalogue. Its name holds the date:

3B-DAY-Ldaily, Late run
GISGeoTIFF edition
IMERGproduct
20261025UTC day
V07Cversion
tifformat

Units

Tenths of a millimetre

Values are stored as whole numbers: 2095 means 209.5 mm. The file says so in its description (ScaleFactor=10), and the app divides by 10.

Missing data

29999

A pixel with no valid estimate holds 29999. The app treats it as missing, never as rain.

Timing

Day D at about 14:00 UTC on D+1

On 9 November 2026 the file of 8 November appeared between 14:03 and 14:13 UTC.

1.4Normal rain: the IMERG daily climatology

The IMERG team publishes a daily climatology: one file per calendar day, holding the average daily rain of that day over 2001–2022, in mm/day.

The file for 21 March, IMERG-Final.CLIM.2001-2022.0321.V07B.tif, is the average of 21 March 2001, 21 March 2002, and so on up to 21 March 2022. A pixel is left missing (−9999.9) when fewer than 20 of the 22 years have data, which happens mostly near the poles.

Why add up daily files? Twenty-two years is a short record, so a single day's climatology is noisy: neighbouring days can differ by about 30%. The IMERG team recommends smoothing it. Adding up the normal over the days of a window does exactly that, and a window that crosses from one month into the next gets the right mix of both.

There is no file for 29 February. Following the IMERG team's advice, the app uses the 28 February normal for that day.

1.5A unit trap: monthly climatology files

NASA also distributes monthly climatology files. They do not hold a monthly total: they hold the average daily rate of that month, in mm/day. The grand climatology holds mm/year.

FileHoldsTo compare with a total over N days
IMERG-Final.CLIM.2001-2022.MMDD.V07B.tifnormal rain of that calendar day, mm/dayadd up the N daily files (what the rolling app does)
IMERG-Final.CLIM.2001-2022.MM.V07B.tifaverage daily rate of that month, mm/daymultiply by N
IMERG-Final.CLIM.200006-202305.V07B.tifnormal rain per year, mm/yearmultiply by N/365

Read as a total, a monthly file underestimates the normal by about 30 times, and every place looks extremely wet. The analyzer app warns when it is given a monthly file and offers BASELINE_MULTIPLIER for this (Tab 7).

Method

Add up the days, then compare

For each window the app adds up the observed rain of its days and the normal rain of the same calendar days, then compares the two sums at every pixel. The window rolls forward by one day every day.

In this section

Below is one real 0.1° pixel of southern Haiti during the flood of late October 2026, with the daily values read from the NASA files. Choose a window length and move the reference day. Watch the shaded window slide, and how the four numbers follow.

Real data: IMERG V07 Late daily files and the IMERG V07B daily climatology at the pixel of each town, 27 September to 30 October 2026. The normal shown here comes from a copy of the climatology stored to 0.01 mm, so it can differ from the maps by 0.1 mm.

2.2The formulas

For a window of N days ending on the reference day d, at one pixel, let Pt be the observed daily rain and Ct the normal daily rain of calendar day t:

Observed and normal over the windowO = ∑t = d−N+1 … d Pt      C̄ = ∑t = d−N+1 … d Ct
Anomaly, mm (rounded to 0.1 mm)A = O − C̄
Percent of normal (rounded to 1%), only where C̄ ≥ 0.5 mm × NR = OC̄ × 100

Worked example, Les Cayes, 3-day window ending 26 October 2026: the daily rain was 52.3, 209.5 and 63.2 mm, so O = 325.0 mm. The normal of those three calendar days adds up to C̄ = 24.3 mm. The anomaly is +300.7 mm and the percent of normal is 1335%: more than thirteen times the usual rain for those days.

2.3Why two measures

Anomaly in mm

How much extra or missing water reached the ground. This is what drives floods and landslides: 150 mm above normal in 3 days is dangerous whatever the percentage. It is produced for 3, 7 and 30 days.

In dry places a big percentage can hide a small amount of water. The mm value keeps the scale honest.

Percent of normal

How unusual the period is for that place and season. 100 = normal, 50 = half, 200 = double. This is the drought and agriculture view. It is produced for 7 and 30 days.

In wet places a large mm anomaly can still be a modest percentage. The percent keeps the comparison local.

2.4Why there is no 3-day percent map by default

Rain is patchy. Over any 3 days most places get little or nothing, and a few places get a lot. The normal, being an average over many years, is spread smoothly over all days.

So on an ordinary 3-day window most pixels sit well below 100% of normal. On the global maps of early November 2026, the typical (median) pixel received about 27% of its normal over 3 days, 55% over 7 days and 87% over 30 days. A 3-day percent map would look dry almost everywhere even when nothing unusual is happening. It can still be requested (PCT_NORMAL with 3, Tab 7).

The 0.5 mm/day threshold

Where the normal is close to zero, as in deserts or a dry season, one shower gives thousands of percent. The percent of normal is therefore left empty where the normal is below 0.5 mm per day on average: 3.5 mm for 7 days, 15 mm for 30 days. On the global maps this leaves about a third of the world empty. The anomaly in mm is always filled.

2.5Missing data and rounding

  • A pixel is empty (NoData) on a map if any of its days, or any of its climatology days, is missing. A partial sum would look drier than reality.
  • A whole window is skipped if one of its daily files is not available, and the run reports which days were missing.
  • Anomaly is rounded to 0.1 mm, percent of normal to 1%. Observed rain itself is only stored to 0.1 mm per day, so more digits would be false precision.
  • Outputs use −9999 as NoData. It is declared in the file, so GIS software and the map styles show it as transparent.
Two apps, one method

From NASA files to styled maps

imerg_rolling_anomaly is built to run unattended every day. spatial_anomaly_analyzer answers one-off questions about any map. Both use the same units, masks and colour styles.

3.2One run of the scheduled app, step by step

imerg_rolling_anomaly

Steps 1 to 4: decide what to do
  1. Read the parametersWhich maps for which windows, the area, the base name of the files. The area is snapped outwards to the 0.1° IMERG grid. Invalid values stop the run with a clear message.
  2. Find the reference dayWithout REFERENCE_DATE, the app searches the IMERG catalogue for daily Late files of the last 7 days and takes the newest. Run at 15:00 UTC on 10 November, that is normally 9 November.
  3. Skip if already doneIt builds the output names for that day. If they all exist, it stops in seconds. This makes frequent scheduled runs cheap.
  4. Check the climatologyEvery calendar day of the longest window needs its climatology file. A missing one stops the run.

imerg_rolling_anomaly

Steps 5 to 8: do it
  1. Import the missing daily filesFiles already in the workspace are reused, so a daily run normally imports one file. Without the reference day's file nothing can be made, and the run stops at once.
  2. Accumulate backwardsFrom the reference day back, each daily file is added to an observed sum and each climatology day to a normal sum. At 3, 7 and 30 days a copy of the sums is kept, so 30 files are read once for all windows.
  3. Compute and add the mapsEach map is written as a compressed Float32 GeoTIFF (EPSG:4326, NoData −9999) with descriptive tags, and added to the workspace with its colour style.
  4. Clean upOnly after every map was added: maps of the same base name older than DAYS_TO_KEEP days, and daily files no longer needed by the longest window, are deleted. Climatology files are never touched.

Why accumulate backwards? All windows end on the same reference day. Walking back from it, the 3-day sum is complete after 3 files, the 7-day sum after 7, the 30-day sum after 30. One pass over the files serves every window.

Every reference day gives new file names. This matters for RISE, which keeps showing a layer once it has read it: a new name for each day is what makes the new maps appear.

The colour styles

Browns mean drier, blue-greens wetter. The "near normal" class is transparent, so only places that stand out are coloured. Missing data is also transparent.

The same anomaly style serves all window lengths, so a 30-day anomaly map is more strongly coloured than a 3-day one: ±5 mm is a small deviation over a month. imerg_pct_change is used by the analyzer app, whose percentage is a change (0 = normal) instead of a percent of normal (100 = normal).

3.4The analyzer app

spatial_anomaly_analyzer takes any input map and any baseline map and returns their difference and percent change, plus optional statistics per region.

  • Grid alignment. The baseline is cropped and resampled (nearest neighbour) on the fly to the exact grid of the input, so a regional input can be compared with a global climatology file.
  • Units. The scale of each file is read from its metadata: IMERG daily files in tenths of mm, NASA climatology in mm. Both can be overridden.
  • Masks. Declared NoData, the IMERG fill value 29999 and the climatology fill value −9999.9 are all treated as missing.
  • Regional statistics. With a shapefile, it adds columns such as abs_mean and perc_max to each polygon and saves a new shapefile.
Absolute anomalyA = X − B
Percent change, where B > 0 and B ≥ MIN_BASELINEP = X − BB × 100

X is the input, B the baseline after scaling and BASELINE_MULTIPLIER. Outputs: Abs_Anomaly_<input> and Perc_Anomaly_<input>.

Cross-check. Run on the 3-day Cumulative and Normal maps of the Haiti example (Tab 5), the analyzer's absolute anomaly is identical to the rolling app's Anomaly map.

3.5The daily schedule

The scheduled app needs no dates: it always finds the newest day by itself. Running it every 6 hours, at 03:00, 09:00, 15:00 and 21:00 UTC, catches each new day soon after NASA publishes it.

  • Expected update: maps for day D are ready at about 15:00–15:30 UTC on day D+1. If NASA is late, the 21:00 run catches it.
  • Missed runs: the next run imports what it needs and builds the most recent day. The days in between are not filled automatically; run the app once by hand with REFERENCE_DATE for each day you need.
  • Size stays constant: with the defaults the workspace holds 30 daily files and 7 days of maps (35 files), plus the climatology.

4.2The event through the rolling window

The same app was run for each reference day from 23 to 30 October, keeping only the 3-day anomaly. This is what a daily schedule would have shown. Press play, or pick a day.

Reference day (3-day window ending on)

The event enters the window, peaks when its three wettest days are all inside (24–26 October), and leaves again. By the window of 28–30 October the peninsula is back to normal. This is why the 3-day map is the flood view, while the 30-day map keeps the event visible for a month.

Know before you use

Strengths and limits

The maps are a consistent, global, daily view of unusual rain. They are satellite estimates, and some situations need care.

In this section

5.1Strengths

Coverage

Everywhere, same method

Every country and ocean on one grid, including places with few or no rain gauges.

Timeliness

Updated every day

Yesterday's rain is in the maps by mid-afternoon UTC, with no manual work.

Context

Local normal built in

Each pixel is compared with its own 22-year normal for the same calendar days.

5.2Limits

LimitWhat it meansWhat to do
Satellite estimateLate has no rain-gauge correction, while the normal is built from gauge-corrected Final data. Globally the two agree well (30-day observed ÷ normal = 1.008), but some regions, such as mountains, coasts and snow-covered ground, can carry a bias.Confirm critical values with local gauges.
ResolutionA 0.1° cell (about 11 km) is an area average. A town can receive more or less than its cell.Read patterns over several cells, not single values.
LatencyThe newest map is for yesterday or the day before, never today.Use forecasts for the coming hours.
Short normal period"Normal" means typical of 2001–2022. Single-day normals are noisy; summing over the window reduces this.Prefer 7 and 30-day percent maps.
Missing daysIf a daily file is never published, every window containing it is skipped until that day leaves the window.Check the run summary for MISSING_DAYS.
Polar regionsIMERG coverage is partial beyond 60° latitude, and the climatology is missing near the poles.Treat high-latitude values with caution.

5.3Reading an empty pixel

  • Transparent on an Anomaly map: either near normal (within ±5 mm) or no data. Point at it, or open the file, to tell them apart: no data is −9999.
  • Transparent on a Percent of normal map: near normal (75–125%), no data, or a normal below 0.5 mm/day. Large empty areas over deserts and dry oceans are the threshold at work.

Get started

Run it yourself

Both apps run in a WASDI workspace. You can use one you already have, or create one from the app's own screen.

In this section

6.1Quick start

  1. Get the climatology. Download the IMERG V07B daily climatology GeoTIFFs from NASA's precipitation climatology page and upload the 365 files IMERG-Final.CLIM.2001-2022.MMDD.V07B.tif to your workspace, keeping their names. This is needed once per workspace.
  2. Open the app. Find imerg_rolling_anomaly in the WASDI marketplace and open it in that workspace.
  3. Set the parameters. Choose the maps, the area and, for a past event, the reference day (examples in 6.4).
  4. Run. The first run imports up to 30 daily files and takes a few minutes; later runs reuse them.
  5. Look at the maps. They appear in the workspace with their colour style. The run summary lists the maps and, for each, the share of valid pixels, the area-weighted mean and the 1st and 99th percentiles.

6.5Scheduling and clean-up

  • Schedule the rolling app every 6 hours (03:00, 09:00, 15:00, 21:00 UTC) with REFERENCE_DATE empty. Runs with nothing new stop in seconds (3.5).
  • Do not change BASE_NAME once scheduled: clean-up only removes maps with the current prefix, so maps with an old prefix would stay forever.
  • Back-filling a day: run once with REFERENCE_DATE set and DELETE_OLD_DAILY_FILES false, so the old date does not remove the daily files of the current windows. A back-filled map older than DAYS_TO_KEEP days is removed again by the next scheduled run.
  • Shared workspaces: for experiments in a workspace that also holds other daily IMERG files, set DELETE_OLD_DAILY_FILES to false and a large DAYS_TO_KEEP, as in the Haiti example.
